issues.body:
## TL;DR

Build RiffleEval as a paired long-context evaluation of coherent stream tracking. Each base item keeps the source text, question, answer, distractors, and token budget fixed while changing document chunks from blocked to riffled order. The primary result is the per-item riffle penalty, sliced by foreign-chunk interference count and token distance.

UncheatableEval is a candidate source feed after revision pinning, token-length filtering, license review, and safety filtering. Its current Marin integration is unsuitable: it downloads a stale GitHub fork whose records are capped at 5,000 characters and supplies no questions or evidence annotations. For v0, use frozen natural documents with exact-answer factual overlays; evaluate a filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` subset as one source arm, beginning with English Wikipedia and permissively licensed documents.

## Description

Long-context evaluations such as NIAH often test retrieval of one conspicuous item from a large context. RiffleEval tests whether a model can maintain several ordered information streams whose chunks repeatedly alternate across a 32K–64K prompt, then reconstruct facts within one stream.

For source document \(D_i = [C_{i,1}, \ldots, C_{i,n}]\), generate a legal merge that preserves chunk order within each source. Every chunk receives an opaque, per-example stream ID and ordinal. Questions and evidence annotations are created and verified against the clean document before riffling.

Each base item produces these conditions:

1. Clean target document, for source-task competence.
2. Blocked full context, with the target and distractor documents contiguous.
3. Riffled full context, with identical content and prompt budget.
4. Adjacent-evidence control for multi-evidence items.

The v0 task families are single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration. Cross-stream joins and continuation NLL remain follow-ups.

The proposed context-length and stream-count matrix is not a full Cartesian product. With 4K–8K source documents, 32K supports roughly 4–8 streams and 64K supports roughly 8–16 streams. Larger documents or additional filler semantics would be required to hold stream count fixed while scaling total context. The generator must reject infeasible cells instead of silently repeating or padding sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

At fixed content and question difficulty, riffling causes a measurable accuracy loss beyond the loss caused by the same blocked distractors. The loss increases with the number of intervening foreign chunks after controlling for absolute token distance. Better long-context checkpoints should move the retention curve toward larger interference counts.

## Status

Background research is complete. No implementation or model run has started.

### Proposed v0

- 250–500 verified base items, expanded into deterministic paired variants.
- 32K and 64K contexts; feasible 4/8/16-stream cells; approximately 512-token chunks.
- Exact short answers with one-evidence and two-evidence overlays.
- Opaque opening and closing markers with tokenizer-balanced random IDs.
- Random and same-domain distractors.
- Native-model score with tools disabled.
- Exact match, per-item riffle penalty, blocked-to-riffled penalty, and retention curves by token distance, interference count, evidence count, and active streams.
- Target-stream extraction and oracle-evidence diagnostics to separate stream selection from reasoning.
- Frozen generator version, seed, source revision/hash, tokenizer, prompt, and structural metadata for every item.

### UncheatableEval corpus decision

Use it as an optional source-discovery and freshness feed. Do not use the published collection as the sole corpus or reuse `experiments/datasets/uncheatable.py`.

The current upstream `-Long` snapshots contain 7,500 records across 15 categories and retain source URL, date, category, `content`, and `untruncated_content`. They provide recent natural interference, but no question, answer, stable ID, evidence span, or hop graph. The dataset card declares no dataset license, and source rights differ by document. AO3 has safety concerns; arbitrary GitHub files need license and secret checks; BBC is a poor redistribution default; PDF extraction can corrupt arXiv text. Freshness only protects models whose training cutoff predates the crawl.

A derived arm must:

- pin the Hugging Face revision and content hash;
- filter on benchmark-tokenizer length, language, quality, and safety;
- record URL, collection date, source category, license, and transformed-text hash;
- begin with English Wikipedia and individually cleared permissive sources;
- exclude BBC and AO3 from v0;
- generate exact-answer overlays and frozen evidence spans against the exact transformed text.

## Background Research Brief

- Effort / stop rule / date: medium; 2026-08-24; stopped when the internal, benchmark, corpus, and contradiction passes no longer changed the v0 recommendation.

### Current Marin context

- #7638 owns RULER integration. RiffleEval should not duplicate its eval harness work.
- #4736 specified the closest reusable data contract: frozen long-document QA items with exact answers, evidence spans, and length bins.
- #7181 found that retained MRCR context reduced final-turn PPL from 21.0855 to 10.4012 at 8,192 tokens. Its extraction PR #7203 closed unmerged, so it is prior evidence rather than current infrastructure.
- #5825 previously built 32K/64K long-document PPL slices; the implementation was later removed by #6633.
- No existing issue or implementation tests repeated switching among several coherent streams.

### External prior art

- [RULER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654) varies context length and task complexity across multi-needle retrieval, variable tracking, aggregation, and QA. RiffleEval adds coherent natural streams and a paired blocked/riffled intervention.
- [MRCR/Michelangelo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) shows that repeated, similar requests and ordinal selection are harder than unique needles. RiffleEval should include similar competing streams and report random/noise floors.
- [NoLiMa](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167) shows that lexical overlap makes retrieval easier and normalizes long-context scores to short-context competence. RiffleEval should vary lexical overlap and reject items with weak clean-document accuracy.
- [BABILong](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf) distributes multi-fact synthetic tasks through natural books. RiffleEval adds several foreground streams, explicit stream identities, and the same task before and after structural transformation.
- [LOFT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121) found that marker and prompt formatting materially affect retrieval. Marker tokenization and query placement must be fixed or explicitly ablated.
- [UncheatableEval](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval) evaluates rolling internet text by NLL. Its freshness method is useful for source discovery; it does not provide RiffleEval annotations.

### Contradiction and shortcut pass

- Random riffles and IDs prevent fixed-order contamination but do not prevent a model from answering public facts from parametric memory. Synthetic counterfactual overlays provide the durable control.
- Opaque IDs expose segmentation but do not prevent keyword search within the target stream. Lexical-overlap and near-neighbor distractor slices remain necessary.
- “Uniform-ish” legal merges do not independently control gap length. Sample examples from explicit interference-count and token-distance strata.
- Marker token lengths can differ across tokenizers and become an unplanned treatment. Balance marker encodings and store their token counts.
- Native QA generation from unannotated documents can admit one-passage shortcuts. Require evidence spans, clean-document verification, and minimal-evidence ablations.

### Recommended next experiments

#### 1. Validate the paired structural signal at 32K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: 100 overlay items, four streams, 512-token chunks; clean, blocked, and riffled conditions on two representative models with different long-context capability.
- Expected signal / falsifier: a nonzero blocked-to-riffled penalty that grows across interference buckets while clean accuracy remains high. Near-zero penalty, floor-level clean accuracy, or prompt-format sensitivity larger than the treatment falsifies the current setup.

#### 2. Add two-evidence integration and 64K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: two controlled facts in widely separated chunks; adjacent-evidence and oracle-extracted-stream baselines; feasible 8/16-stream cells.
- Expected signal / falsifier: two-evidence retention degrades faster than one-evidence retention while oracle extraction recovers most accuracy. Failure of the oracle indicates base reasoning or question-construction problems.

#### 3. Compare source pools

- Minimum experiment / baseline: matched overlays over a pinned filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` arm and one stable, license-cleared long-document corpus.
- Expected signal / falsifier: model ranking and riffle penalty remain stable across source pools. Large domain-specific reversals require a multi-corpus benchmark or removal of the unstable source.

### Source ledger

| Source | Type | Location | Claim used for | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RULER | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654 | complexity axes and baselines | high | nearest variable-tracking precedent |
| Michelangelo / MRCR | paper and official code | https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640 | repeated similar needles and order | high | conversation format differs from riffled documents |
| NoLiMa | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167 | lexical-overlap shortcut and retention normalization | high | single-association retrieval |
| BABILong | paper | https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf | distributed multi-fact reasoning in natural text | high | one background stream |
| LOFT | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121 | formatting and identifier sensitivity | high | fixed retrieval corpora |
| UncheatableEval | official repo and dataset | https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07-Long | source schema, freshness, and corpus limitations | high | no dataset-level license or QA annotations |
| Marin #4736 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4736 | QA manifest and evidence schema | high | closed before implementation |
| Marin #7638 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7638 | active RULER scope | high | avoid duplicate harness work |

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

🤖 Scaling-ladder analysis for the **535B-A23B, 18T-token** hero. The ladder trains one uniform hero EP recipe at five widths; four rungs finished and the d2048 rung crashed at ~81%. Fitting a power law across the rungs (`L = 1.5 + A·C^-α`, compute excludes lm_head) and extrapolating to the hero's compute predicts a final **dropless paloma macro-loss ≈ 2.04**.

**Hero prediction by training percentile** — the four measured rungs plus the d6144 hero prediction at every 5% (dashed/hollow = extrapolated).
![hero prediction by percentile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/hero_prediction_by_percentile.png)

**Per-5% scaling-law fits (log-log)** — one power-law fit per training fraction; the crimson points trace the hero prediction out to hero-scale compute, ending at 2.039 @100%.
![scaling law fits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_scaling_laws.png)

**Method check** — a linear extrapolation from each finished rung's 60–80% window predicts its own 100% dropless macro-loss to within ~0.003–0.004 (consistently a hair optimistic, since the curve flattens under cosine decay).
![60-80 extrapolation vs actual](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_extrapolation_60_80.png)

**Full-granularity training cross-entropy** — every step, with the datamix phase-2 boundary at 80% (a small loss bump is visible in every rung at that point).
![training cross-entropy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/d23e6e9c3673435fb82d83aa6c51a607d0da6009/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/scaling_ladder_figs/ladder_train_ce_fullres.png)

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

Thanks for sharing this work.  
I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body: @windsornguyen we can share lots of metadata for data mix but we're unable to grant direct access to data. What are you looking for?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Marin has no way to mark a test as needing a GPU, a minimum device count, or a specific accelerator. Some accelerator tests skip invisibly in CI as a result, and the two that need real device topology were written outside pytest entirely.

`tests/test_utils.py` provides `skip_if_no_tpu` and nothing equivalent for GPUs or device counts. The root `pyproject.toml` markers are `slow`, `integration`, `data_integration`, `cluster`, `requires_cluster`, `docker`, and `manual`; none describes hardware. `tests/cluster/conftest.py` names two clusters, `MARIN_TPU_CLUSTER` and `MARIN_GPU_CLUSTER = "cw-us-east-02a"`, with no entry for the GB200 cluster `cw-us-east-08a`.

Two tests in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py` check the ragged all-to-all MoE backend against a dense reference and run nowhere:

```
uv run python -m pytest lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py -rs -k "ragged or granular or clip"
...
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[ragged_all_to_all]
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_reports_positive_drop_count_in_ragged_a2a_when_over_capacity
5 passed, 2 skipped
```

They skip on `requires an even number of >=2 devices`, and forcing two CPU devices hits the next guard, `ragged_all_to_all is not implemented on XLA:CPU`. Every job in `.github/workflows/` runs on `ubuntu-latest`. The five that pass cover lowering, offset arithmetic against a NumPy simulation of the collective, and capacity clipping in isolation. None runs the real collective or the SM100 expert kernels.

The root `addopts` does not include `-rs`, so these skips never appear in CI output. A green run with full coverage and a green run with no ragged coverage look identical.

Both files that need real accelerator topology avoided pytest. `lib/iris/tests/e2e/gpu_gang_smoke.py` is a standalone `__main__` script with `--target kind|coreweave` and `--i-understand-the-cost`; it mock-labels kind nodes to simulate an NVLink domain instead of requiring one. `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ragged_ep_check.py` (PR #8549) submits a 4-GPU GB200 job, computes a pass/fail verdict, and raises on failure, but sits under `experiments/` with no scheduled caller.

Two cases need different mechanisms. A test like the levanter one needs N local devices inside the pytest process. A test like `ragged_ep_check` needs no local hardware: it submits a job whose constraint rides in `ResourceConfig.with_gpu("GB200", count=4, ...)`, so what it needs is a cluster fixture and a way to declare that the run is expensive.

#7242 delivered `tests/cluster/`, the `cluster` marker, and `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` for smokes that submit real jobs. It left open which hardware a test needs and what a test that cannot get that hardware should do.

Done when:

- A test can declare a local device requirement and skip with a named reason instead of an ad-hoc in-file guard.
- Skipped tests are visible in CI output.
- A job-submitting test can target the GB200 cluster through a fixture, and its cost is expressible on the test rather than only in the workflow.
- One existing case is ported as the reference: the levanter ragged EP tests, or `ragged_ep_check.py`.

comments.body:
🤖 Correction to this issue's premise, found while acting on it in #8549.

It says `tests/cluster/` "covers submitting a job to a standing cluster" and that the gap is a GB200 lane and a cost tier on the existing workflow. The workflow no longer exists. #8605 deleted `.github/workflows/marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` on 2026-08-22, and its commit message gives the reason:

> Marin Cluster Smoke had zero successful scheduled runs: all 38 runs from July 17 through August 23 were cancelled around its 100-minute timeout. The workflow and its Grafana lane are deleted. The underlying tests remain directly runnable through the cluster-test runbook.

So nothing runs the `cluster` marker at all now, and this issue covers restoring a runner rather than extending one. The two other gaps it names are unaffected: there is still no way to declare a local device requirement, and `addopts` still carries no `-rs`, so skipped tests stay invisible.

One gap it named is now closed. #8549 moved the 4-GPU ragged transport gate to `tests/cluster/grug/test_ragged_ep_check.py`. That needed only a constant naming the GB200 peer, because `cw-us-east-08a` is already a federation peer of the marin hub and `target_cluster` is a `ResourceConfig` field, so `iris_client` works unchanged. No new fixture was required after all.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting my comment above, which was too absolute. "No workflow runs the `cluster` marker" is accurate; "accelerator tests have no automated vehicle" was not.

Scheduled GPU work does run. `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` fires daily at 10:00 UTC against `cw-us-west-04a`, sets `CANARY_ACCELERATOR: gpu`, and runs `python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry` on 8x H100 through Iris, with `scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py` asserting the result. That is a real accelerator smoke on a daily cron. It is not pytest and carries no marker.

`iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` looks like a second GPU lane and is not one. It runs `pytest tests/test_integration_test.py -m integration` on PRs touching `lib/iris/**`, and the workflow comment says it submits "against the shared H100" — but the jobs `tests/integration_test.py` submits are `ResourceConfig.with_cpu()` with `require_accelerator=False`. It exercises a CoreWeave-hosted controller, not a GPU.

The deleted `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` had two jobs, not one. `marin-tpu-smokes` ran on the schedule; `marin-gpu-smokes` was `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.run_gpu`, so it never ran on a cron at all. The 38 timed-out scheduled runs the deleting commit cites were the TPU job. Standing-cluster GPU tests were therefore never automatic, before or after #8605.

So the gap this issue describes is sharper than "no runner": **no pytest marker anywhere selects GPU work.** The `cluster` marker has no workflow, and the `integration` marker runs only CPU jobs. Every GPU assertion in CI today lives in the canary ferry, outside pytest.

Two facts worth having when someone picks this up. The canary already parameterizes the accelerator (`CANARY_GPU_TYPE`, documented as "H100, GH200, B200", plus `CANARY_GPU_COUNT` and `CANARY_GPU_REPLICAS`), so scheduling GPU work of a given shape from Actions is solved machinery rather than something to build. And `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` and `iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` share the concurrency group `iris-coreweave-ci-shared` because they contend for one host, so any added lane needs a capacity story and not only a config entry.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Background
In #6070, the [PPL circuit-coverage gap dashboard](https://marin.community/analysis/ppl-circuit-coverage-gap/) showed that Marin 32B is much worse than Qwen3 32B at basic "code interpretation" skills: arithmetic, manipulating strings into tokens, exact character/index tracking, and other short deterministic continuations.

We suspect these skills are also important for agentic tasks. Agents need to read observations, preserve exact identifiers, transform text, update state, compare quantities, follow formats, and manipulate tool outputs. Many of these skills are simple in the sense that they are fully algorithmic and should not require a lot of reasoning, but they still need to be reliable.

We want to identify other tasks that seem important for agents and that models may not learn automatically from existing data, mostly web text and code. These tasks are likely to involve textual manipulation, arithmetic, format understanding, span selection, and state tracking, but they can involve other basic algorithmic skills as well.

## Description
Collect short no-code proposals for additional PPL circuit/basic-functionality tasks before implementing them. These tasks do not have to be code-related. The point is to identify small skills an agent should need for reliable tool use, reasoning over observations, formatting, state tracking, and code or data interpretation.

Post one comment per proposed task or small family on this issue using this template:

````markdown
## Proposed task
<short name, e.g. json_path_lookup, loop_counter_trace, calendar_delta, or table_cell_lookup>

## Skill being tested
<the concrete ability: indexing, escaping, stack state, operator precedence, argument binding, table lookup, unit conversion, date arithmetic, format following, etc.>

## Three examples
```text
<compact example 1, including final answer>
<compact example 2, including final answer>
<compact example 3, including final answer>
```

## Failure modes
<what a model might get wrong: off-by-one, byte/char confusion, quote escaping, state update order, unit mismatch, row/column mixup, leakage from task phrasing, etc.>

## Why an agent should need this skill
<how this primitive shows up in tool use, reading observations, updating state, planning, working with user data, or interpreting code/logs/UI text>

## Why ordinary pretraining may not teach it reliably
<why passive pretraining might underrepresent this skill: few explicit inputs paired with outputs, answers hidden in runtime/tool behavior, sparse edge cases, docs explain the rule but do not provide many executed examples, etc.>

## Implementation notes
<optional: useful metadata to store, edge cases to include, or related task family>
````

Example of a fully fleshed-out proposal, based on a task already implemented in `experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py`:

````markdown
## Proposed task
string_slicing

## Skill being tested
Python-style string indexing and slicing: start/stop/step handling, omitted characters, Unicode codepoint indexing, and the difference between the prompt prefix and the final answer.

## Three examples
```text
text = "abcdef"; text[1:5:2] -> 'bd'
text = "marin"; text[0:4:1] -> 'mari'
text = "́kder/ejehcp"; text[6:11:1] -> 'ejehc'
```

## Failure modes
Off-by-one start/stop errors, treating the stop index as inclusive, ignoring step, reversing the slice direction, confusing Unicode characters with UTF-8 bytes, copying the entire input string, or including explanatory text instead of only the final Python `repr` answer.

## Why an agent should need this skill
Agents routinely have to extract spans from tool output, logs, file paths, UI text, and user-provided strings. Slicing is a compact proxy for precise span selection: if a model cannot reliably take `text[start:stop:step]`, it will also struggle to copy the right substring from observations, preserve exact identifiers, or reason about offsets in code and data.

## Why ordinary pretraining may not teach it reliably
Pretraining corpora contain many slice expressions, but usually not paired with their executed result. Documentation explains the rule, and tests sometimes include expected outputs, but random slices over arbitrary strings are sparse. Edge cases like non-unit steps, Unicode combining marks, and stop-index exclusivity are especially unlikely to appear as dense input-output practice.

## Implementation notes
Generate short strings with varied punctuation and Unicode, choose valid `start`, `stop`, and `step` values, store those values plus the source text in metadata, and validate the target as `repr(text[start:stop:step])`. The supervised row should put completed few-shot lines in `input`, leave the held-out line ending in `-> `, and put only the quoted slice plus newline in `output`.
````

Good first proposal areas:

- Python/JSON literal lookup and re-emission.
- Regex-lite capture groups and substitutions.
- Small loop/state traces.
- Path, URL, or import-name normalization.
- Date/time arithmetic and formatting.
- CSV/TSV quoting and escaping.
- Boolean/operator precedence.
- Function-call argument binding with defaults.
- Table cell lookup and row/column selection.
- Unit conversion and quantity comparison.
- Checklist/state update after a sequence of actions.

Keep examples compact and avoid telegraphing the task with labels like `Task:` or `Final answer:`. A good proposal should be easy for a human to solve, easy to generate deterministically, and easy to validate from metadata.

### Definition of Done
- At least ten proposal comments are posted on this issue using the template above.
- Each proposal comment includes three compact examples, failure modes, why an agent should need the skill, and why ordinary pretraining may not teach it reliably.
- Accepted proposals are promoted into implementation work on #6236.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Finish the token-native RL rollout data plane for Levanter and vLLM inference contexts. OpenAI compatibility is useful for testing, but the RL path should preserve tokenization identity, policy/version identity, sampled tokens, logprobs, masks, prompt/completion boundaries, finish reasons, and replay metadata without reconstructing token IDs from text.

PR #6186 (`codex/rl-token-rollout-api`, head `c4ba37bda1f429700528a442e2f18e906b96d1b9`) now carries the active implementation slice and has all visible checks green. It includes typed token rollout contracts, vLLM and Levanter token-native context methods, MathEnv and MockEnv token-native adapters, policy/checkpoint identity, tokenizer/chat-template replay identity, structured failure envelopes, stored rollout trace metadata, MoE router/expert replay metadata, OpenAI-shaped identity preservation, and completion-mask preservation through training batch construction.

### PrimeIntellect Decision
Do not block #6186 on converting `PrimeIntellectEnv` to the token-native path. Keep `PrimeIntellectEnv` OpenAI/verifiers-compatible for this PR stack because verifiers stop/tool-routing behavior still needs a concrete tokenized adapter design. This is acceptable for the current slice because #6186 preserves attached `response_token_ids` when present and carries tokenizer/policy replay identity through the shared OpenAI-shaped rollout path.

After #6185/#6186 land, split PrimeIntellect/verifiers work into smaller follow-ups: decide which verifier environments can expose tokenized prompts/results, centralize token-native versus OpenAI-compatible capability selection, add cross-environment roundtrip coverage, and turn missing-token or missing-logprob cases into explicit structured failures or loud errors.

### Definition of Done
- [x] vLLM and Levanter contexts expose the token-native rollout API behind stable types.
- [x] MathEnv and MockEnv can consume token-native outputs when the backend supports them.
- [x] Partial failures have structured envelopes for missing backend generations.
- [x] Integration coverage verifies IDs, boundaries, logprobs, masks, tokenizer identity, and policy metadata survive the round trip for the implemented paths.
- [x] PrimeIntellectEnv has a token-native path, or an explicit design decision documents why it remains OpenAI-compatible while preserving attached token IDs and replay identity.
- [ ] The rollout data plane lands after the serving stack it depends on, or maintainers accept the current stack ordering.

### Current Next Step
#6186 is the main token-native rollout PR and is green. The remaining blocker for this issue is stack acceptance/landing order: #6186 should land after the serving stack it depends on, or maintainers should explicitly accept the current stack ordering. PrimeIntellect-specific token-native work should be a follow-up after #6186 lands, not a blocker for this PR.

### Parent
- #6227

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Fetch issue, parent #6227, and predecessor PR #6186
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no parallel PRs; only #6186 in flight)
- [x] Scope assessment — too large for a single agent PR, blocked on #6186
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach for human review
- [ ] Re-engage once #6186 lands and a subtask is carved out

# Research

The token-native rollout API does not exist on `main` yet — it lands with PR #6186 (open, +2517/-24, 21 files), which adds `TokenRolloutRequest`/`TokenRolloutResult` to `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/types.py`, `generate_token_rollouts` on `BaseInferenceContext`, and concrete vLLM + Levanter implementations wired through `MathEnv` and `MockEnv`. This issue is the follow-on hardening pass: extend the typed path to PrimeIntellectEnv (still on OpenAI client + BPE round-trip), define structured partial-failure envelopes, add worker-level backend selection, and write cross-backend integration tests that assert tokenizer/policy identity, prompt/completion boundaries, logprobs, masks, and finish reasons survive the round trip.

The PrimeIntellect path is the largest remaining gap: it still calls `inference_ctx.openai_client()` and reconstructs token IDs via `process_vllm_chat_results` using `tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids()` — exactly the lossy reconstruction the issue calls out. Worker-level selection is also unsettled: `rollout_worker.py` (1098 lines on `main`) does not yet branch on whether a backend supports token-native rollouts.

**Relevant code**
- [`prime_intellect_env.py#L74-L194`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/prime_intellect_env.py#L74-L194) — verifiers path: OpenAI client + token-ID reconstruction
- [`inference_ctx/base.py#L65-L81`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/base.py#L65-L81) — current BPE vocab round-trip the issue wants to replace
- [`inference/types.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/types.py) — where #6186 adds the typed contracts (+309 lines)
- [`rollout_worker.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_worker.py) — where worker-level backend selection would live
- PR #6186 — foundational contracts and MathEnv/MockEnv slice (open)

# Proposed Approach

Hold for #6186 to land, then split into four sequenced PRs against the landed contracts. Doing it in one PR now would conflict with the 21 files #6186 touches and would freeze the contract before review feedback settles.

1. **PrimeIntellectEnv token-native path.** Replace `vf_env.generate(...)` + `process_vllm_chat_results` with a verifiers adapter that calls `inference_ctx.generate_token_rollouts(...)` and constructs `Rollout`s directly from the typed result. Keep the OpenAI client only for environments that don't yet expose tokens. Gate on `inference_ctx.supports_token_rollouts()` (new capability flag on `BaseInferenceContext`) and fall back loudly — `raise`, not silent OpenAI fallback. ~150 LOC + tests.

2. **Structured partial-failure envelopes.** Introduce `TokenRolloutOutcome = Success(TokenRolloutResult) | Failure(reason, request_id, partial_tokens?)` (frozen dataclass union, not booleans). vLLM raises today on per-prompt failures inside a batch; surface them per-request instead so a single OOM/truncation does not drop the whole batch. Wire `rollout_worker` to count `Failure` envelopes into metrics and log structured `finish_reason` for length truncations. ~200 LOC + tests.

3. **Worker-level backend selection.** Add `RolloutWorker._pick_rollout_path(env, inference_ctx) -> RolloutPath` returning `TOKEN_NATIVE` vs `OPENAI_COMPAT`, driven by the env declaring capability and the backend supporting it. Removes the per-env branching that #6186 inlines into `MathEnv`/`MockEnv`. ~80 LOC + tests.

4. **Cross-backend integration coverage.** One parameterized test file `tests/rl/test_token_rollout_roundtrip.py` running the same prompt through (vLLM stub, Levanter, MockEnv) and asserting: tokenizer-id equality, prompt/completion boundary offsets, logprob length == response length, mask shape, finish_reason preserved, policy version + tokenizer name persisted on the result. Reuse fixtures from `tests/rl/test_levanter_token_rollouts.py` and `tests/rl/test_vllm_token_rollouts.py` introduced in #6186. ~250 LOC.

Open questions for the maintainer before implementation:
- Should `PrimeIntellectEnv` keep an OpenAI fallback for verifier envs that need server-side tool routing, or hard-fail on backends without token rollouts?
- Where should the capability flag live — `BaseInferenceContext.supports_token_rollouts: bool` property, or a `Capabilities` dataclass returned by `get_capabilities()`?
- For partial failures, do we want per-request envelopes or a `BatchResult{successes, failures}` shape that keeps batch semantics intact?

Ready to take any one of (1)-(4) as a standalone PR once #6186 merges and these design points are resolved.

spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Explain and reduce the v6e prefill-heavy gap for `prefill_b8_i2048_o128_n1`.

Historical comparison row: Levanter `1006.83` decode tok/s and `17116.08` total tok/s versus vLLM `1262.90` decode tok/s and `21469.31` total tok/s, ratio `0.797`. That measured Levanter row had prefill chunks `4096,4096,4096,4096` and one decode iteration with `0.802s` total, `0.623s` device, `0.178s` host, and `0.174s` submit.

The corrected Levanter-only diagnostic completed at `/dlwh/qwen3-v6e8-prefilldiag-drain-prefill-b8-i2048-o128-n1-20260606-1532` from PR #6185 commit `82bb6dbfb`. It validated diagnostic prefill drain and produced `1022` decode iteration tokens for normal, `no_lm_head`, and `lm_head_no_sampling` rows.

Important interpretation correction: production `decode_submit_seconds` was previously measured from the start of the outer iteration before prefill drain, so the `0.174s`/`0.184s` submit field included prefill admission work. PR #6185 commit `dd993c03c` moved the submit timer to immediately before `_run_generation_loop(...)`, commit `6d74fc7ea` added decode iteration/device throughput fields, and commit `f55913d1` now separates prefill drain from the generation loop with `prefill_drain_*`, `generation_*`, and derived `generation_tokens_per_second` benchmark fields.

Corrected backend=both row: `/dlwh/qwen3-v6e8-prefillcorr-20260607-0023` completed successfully from #6185 head `91f6ec06a`. vLLM measured `1212.15` decode tok/s and `20606.54` total tok/s. Levanter measured `898.94` decode tok/s and `15282.00` total tok/s, ratio `0.742`, target fail. The corrected Levanter fields available in that run show prefill chunks `4096,4096,4096,4096`, prefill admission wall times `0.060,0.055,0.055,0.055s`, decode iteration `0.852s` total / `0.677s` device / `0.174s` host / `0.002s` submit / `0.002s` extract, `1022` decode iteration tokens, `1200.223` decode-iteration tok/s, and `1509.350` device tok/s. Because that row predates `f55913d1`, it does not yet include the new generation-only token/time split.


Post-`f55913d1` backend=both row: `/dlwh/qwen3-v6e8-prefillpostsplit-20260607-0419` completed successfully from #6185 head `d63d1edf`. vLLM measured `1264.03` decode tok/s and `21488.50` total tok/s. Levanter measured `957.72` decode tok/s and `16281.24` total tok/s, ratio `0.758`, target fail. The new split shows hot prefill chunks `4096,4096,4096,4096` with prefill wall times `0.060,0.056,0.056,0.056s`, decode iteration `0.800s` total / `0.623s` device / `0.177s` host / `0.002s` submit / `0.002s` extract, `1022` decode iteration tokens, `0.171s` prefill drain for `6` tokens, and `0.629s` generation for `1016` tokens. Derived throughput: `1277.749` decode-iteration tok/s, `1639.896` decode-device tok/s, and `1614.816` generation tok/s.

Follow-up code changes:
- #6185 commit `f7275e5a` stops logging full `InferenceRequest` dataclasses at INFO and instead logs bounded request metadata. In the prefill-heavy measured row, the old path serialized eight 2048-token prompt lists before the first prefill admission; this was a concrete host-side measured-path overhead source. Validation passed with inference-server pytest (`19 passed, 1 skipped`) plus focused pre-commit/Pyrefly on the touched files.
- #6185 commit `f55913d1` adds per-iteration `prefill_drain_seconds_per_iteration`, `prefill_drain_tokens_per_iteration`, `generation_seconds_per_iteration`, `generation_host_seconds_per_iteration`, `generation_tokens_per_iteration`, and `generation_tokens_per_second` to avoid conflating prefill-drain work with generation-loop throughput in future #6229 rows. Validation passed with `test_engine.py` and `test_qwen3_tpu_inference_parity_bench.py` (`63 passed`) plus focused pre-commit/Pyrefly.

Current interpretation: the remaining failure is attributed to end-to-end prefill-heavy wall-clock overhead rather than a proven decode-device regression. The issue remains open as a performance target because the post-`f55913d1` row still fails the end-to-end parity target at `0.758`, even though generation-only throughput is above the vLLM decode row. The remaining question is whether to optimize hot prefill/admission/serving wall-clock for this weak prefill-heavy regime, or deprioritize it relative to the core RL rollout rows.

### Definition of Done
- [x] Rerun one corrected Levanter-only diagnostic on the fixed harness.
- [x] Attribute the original row enough to avoid a false decode-kernel conclusion: the old submit timing was contaminated by prefill-drain work, and new benchmark fields separate prefill-drain, generation-loop, device, host, submit, and extraction timing.
- [x] Collect a post-`f55913d1` row for `prefill_b8_i2048_o128_n1` if this regime remains a priority, so the result includes `generation_*` and `prefill_drain_*` fields after bounded request logging.
- [ ] Decide the next optimization or close/deprioritize this issue based on that post-`f55913d1` row: prefill/host accounting, page/admission settings, or no further work if the row is acceptable for RL rollout priorities.
- [x] Update the epic and handoff with terminal job results from the completed diagnostics/reruns.

### Current Next Step
Do not launch another TPU run automatically. The next step is a decision, not more evidence collection: either optimize the remaining hot prefill/admission/serving wall-clock overhead for this regime, or close/deprioritize it if core RL rollout rows matter more than prefill-heavy parity. The post-split row should be interpreted using `generation_tokens_per_second=1614.816`, `prefill_drain_seconds_per_iteration=0.171`, and `generation_host_seconds_per_iteration=0.006`, not only the end-to-end `decode_tokens_per_second=957.72`.

- #6227

spillover_issues.title: [levanter] Optimize v6e prefill-heavy decode gap

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
Imagine the following situation: someone running on interactive queue requests a v4-16 and at the time of their request, this is schedulable. Then, someone running on the production queue requests a v4-8 but we are now at capacity.

In an ideal world, where the slices were fungible, we'd want to preempt the interactive queue job, kill the v4-16, and spin up a v4-8 to serve the production user. 

On our spot/preemptible capacity, we don't do this because there is no guarantee that killing the v4-16 will allow us to spin up the v4-8.

However, on our limited reserved capacity we can guarantee this since the compute is fungible up to our cap.

As such, specifically for the reserved compute, we should preempt lower priority jobs to serve higher priority jobs even if the chip types dont match.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and walk the Iris scheduler preemption code
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (none found; #6086 covers unrelated reconcile findings)
- [x] Decide scope — design change, too large for an agent PR
- [x] Post research + proposed approach for human review

# Research

Today's preemption pass hard-gates victims by `device_variant`. Solo preemptors only evict solo victims of the same variant ([`scheduling_policy.py#L560`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling_policy.py#L560)); coscheduled preemptors only evict a whole slice of the same variant whose member count ≥ preemptor's ([`scheduling_policy.py#L622-L628`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling_policy.py#L622-L628)). Neither path knows whether the victim's worker is on reserved vs preemptible/on-demand capacity — `RunningTaskInfo` carries `device_variant` but no `capacity_type` ([`scheduling_policy.py#L94-L111`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling_policy.py#L94-L111)), and the `preemptible` worker attribute lives on `WorkerCapacity.attributes` but isn't read in the preemption pass.

The same-variant gate is correct on spot/preemptible — eviction frees a fixed slice shape the autoscaler can't reshape on demand. On reserved capacity it's over-conservative for the reason in the issue: chips are fungible up to cap.

**Relevant code**
- [`scheduling_policy.py#L538-L592`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling_policy.py#L538-L592) — `_preempt_solo` same-variant gate
- [`scheduling_policy.py#L595-L638`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling_policy.py#L595-L638) — `_preempt_coscheduled` variant + slice-shape gate
- [`scheduling_policy.py#L476-L535`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling_policy.py#L476-L535) — `get_running_tasks_with_band_and_value` (RunningTaskInfo source; no capacity_type)
- [`constraints.py#L1147-L1154`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/constraints.py#L1147-L1154) — `preemptible` attribute injection from `capacity_type`
- [`autoscaler/routing.py#L232`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/routing.py#L232) — autoscaler routes demand per scale group's `capacity_type`

# Proposed approach (design change — needs human review before PR)

1. Plumb `capacity_type` (or just `is_reserved`) onto `RunningTaskInfo` by reading `WellKnownAttribute.PREEMPTIBLE` (and capacity_type if available) from the worker attributes already in the scheduling snapshot. Symmetrically tag each `PreemptionCandidate` with whether the preemptor is targeting reserved (it already constrains via `preemptible_constraint`, so this is mostly extracting the existing constraint).
2. Relax the variant gate in `_preempt_solo` and `_preempt_coscheduled` to: `wanted_variant == victim_variant` OR `preemptor_targets_reserved AND victim_on_reserved AND same_reserved_pool`. The hypothetical-capacity check stays — solo cross-variant preemption only works if the freed worker can actually host the request post-eviction (mostly meaningful for CPU/RAM-bound bin packing; TPU slices are whole-worker-owned and need pool reshaping).
3. Coscheduled cross-variant is the harder case: a v4-8 preemptor evicting a v4-16 slice can't land this tick because TPU shape is a property of the physical slice, not the worker. The realistic plan is "evict now, autoscaler reshapes the reserved pool, preemptor lands next tick" — i.e. relax the gate and rely on the autoscaler/provider to serve the new shape from freed reserved cap.

# Open design questions (block implementation)

- **Granularity of "reserved pool"**: is fungibility "all reserved scale groups" or "within one scale group"? Scale-group routing today is per-group ([`autoscaler/routing.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/routing.py)), and a v4 reservation isn't fungible with a v5p one — needs an explicit "reserved-pool key" (region + family + cap-pool id?) carried on workers and on the preemptor's matching worker set.
- **Thrash safety**: today eviction credit is computed against `WorkerCapacity` deltas. If we evict a v4-16 and the provider can't actually re-provision a v4-8 (cap already claimed by other reservations, regional shortage), we kill an interactive job for nothing and the preemptor re-fires next tick. Gate the cross-variant eviction on a dry-run autoscaler-can-serve check, or add a per-victim cooldown.
- **Scope of relaxation**: does cross-variant apply only when the preemptor is PRODUCTION evicting INTERACTIVE/BATCH, or also INTERACTIVE→BATCH? The issue's example is PRODUCTION→INTERACTIVE; I'd start there.

# Sizing

Implementation is ~200–400 LOC plus tests, plus a short design doc in `.agents/projects/` covering the three questions above. Not a self-contained agent fix — flagging for human review.
